title: How do parallel transactions cause deadlocks, and how do you handle them in Spring (lock ordering, optimistic locking, retry, SKIP LOCKED)?
shortTitle: How do you handle parallel transaction deadlocks?

s1_definition.profdef: Deadlocks occur when two transactions hold locks and wait for each other's locks — circular wait. Four handling strategies: (1) **Consistent lock ordering** — all threads lock rows in same order (no cycle). (2) **Optimistic locking** (`@Version`) — no locks held, retry on `ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException`. (3) **`@Retryable`** — auto-retry on deadlock/optimistic lock failure with backoff. (4) **SKIP LOCKED** — `SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` skips rows locked by others instead of waiting — enables queue-style concurrent processing without deadlocks. Best for job queues where work items can be processed in any order.
s1_definition.analogy: Deadlock = two tellers each holding one key, waiting for the other's. Fix options: (1) Always grab keys in alphabetical order. (2) Don't grab keys — work optimistically, retry if someone else changed the data. (3) Auto-retry when conflict happens. (4) Skip locked items — "that account is busy, I'll process the next one."
s1_definition.oneliner: Lock ordering prevents deadlocks. Optimistic locking avoids locks entirely. SKIP LOCKED skips busy rows for queue processing. @Retryable for automatic recovery.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Deadlocks occur when two transactions hold locks and wait for each other's locks — circular wait. Four handling strategies: (1) **Consistent lock ordering** — all threads lock rows in same order (no cycle). (2) **Optimistic locking** (`@Version`) — no locks held, retry on `ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException`. (3) **`@Retryable`** — auto-retry on deadlock/optimistic lock failure with backoff. (4) **SKIP LOCKED** — `SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` skips rows locked by others instead of waiting — enables queue-style concurrent processing without deadlocks. Best for job queues where work items can be processed in any order.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Deadlock = two tellers each holding one key, waiting for the other's. Fix options: (1) Always grab keys in alphabetical order. (2) Don't grab keys — work optimistically, retry if someone else changed the data. (3) Auto-retry when conflict happens. (4) Skip locked items — "that account is busy, I'll process the next one."

**One line to remember:** Lock ordering prevents deadlocks. Optimistic locking avoids locks entirely. SKIP LOCKED skips busy rows for queue processing. @Retryable for automatic recovery.

sections.s2_technical:
A deadlock is a circular wait: transaction one holds a lock on row A and wants row B, while transaction two holds row B and wants row A. Neither can proceed, so the database detects the cycle and kills one transaction. There are four complementary ways to handle this in Spring. The first is consistent lock ordering: if every thread always locks rows in the same order, for example sorted by account ID, no cycle can form. The second is optimistic locking with a `@Version` column, where no row lock is held at all; instead a concurrent change is caught at write time as `ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException` and the operation is retried.

The third is `@Retryable`, which automatically retries a method on a deadlock or optimistic-lock exception with a backoff delay, for example `@Retryable(retryFor = CannotAcquireLockException.class, maxAttempts = 3)`. The fourth is `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, which skips rows another transaction already locked instead of waiting for them. This is ideal for a job queue: each worker grabs the next unlocked item, so there is no contention, no waiting, and no duplicate processing. For example, a repository query `SELECT * FROM pending_payments WHERE status='PENDING' ORDER BY created_at FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1` lets many workers drain the queue in parallel. A senior nuance: pessimistic locking with SKIP LOCKED suits high-contention queues, optimistic locking suits rare conflicts, and consistent ordering is the baseline discipline that prevents the deadlock in the first place.
sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's payment queue processor picks pending payments from a table.** Multiple instances process concurrently. Without SKIP LOCKED, two instances pick the SAME payment → duplicate processing OR deadlock. With SKIP LOCKED, each instance skips rows locked by others and picks the next available one — zero contention, zero deadlocks, zero duplicates.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a queue with PAY-001 through PAY-005 in PENDING status, drained by two worker instances running concurrently.

**Step 1.** Worker-1 begins a transaction and runs `findNextPendingSkipLocked()`, which issues `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1`. It locks and returns PAY-001.

**Step 2.** At almost the same moment Worker-2 runs the same query. Because PAY-001 is already locked, SKIP LOCKED makes the database skip it and return the next unlocked row, PAY-002. Neither worker waits for the other.

**Step 3.** Worker-1 processes PAY-001 (debits the account, marks it PROCESSED) and commits, releasing the lock. Worker-2 independently processes PAY-002 and commits.

**Step 4.** Both workers loop and call the query again; Worker-1 picks PAY-003, Worker-2 picks PAY-004, and one of them later picks PAY-005. Every item is processed exactly once.

**Step 5.** No two workers ever selected the same row, so there were zero duplicates and zero deadlocks. Had a genuine write-write conflict occurred on an optimistic path, `@Retryable` would have re-run the method after a short backoff.

```
INFO  [worker-1] QueueProcessorService - locked PAY-001 (SKIP LOCKED), processed, COMMIT
INFO  [worker-2] QueueProcessorService - PAY-001 busy → picked PAY-002, processed, COMMIT
INFO  [worker-1] QueueProcessorService - picked PAY-003 ... no duplicates, no deadlocks
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ SKIP LOCKED — concurrent queue processing ═══

  Instance-1: SELECT * FROM pending_payments WHERE status='PENDING'
              ORDER BY created_at FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1
    → Picks PAY-001 (LOCKED)

  Instance-2 (simultaneous):
    → PAY-001 is LOCKED → SKIP! → Picks PAY-002 (LOCKED)

  Instance-3 (simultaneous):
    → PAY-001, PAY-002 LOCKED → SKIP! → Picks PAY-003

  Result: 3 instances process 3 DIFFERENT payments in parallel.
    No deadlock. No waiting. No duplicate processing. (Recommended) 

  ═══ OPTIMISTIC LOCKING + @Retryable ═══

  Thread-1: SELECT payment WHERE id='PAY-004' → version=0
  Thread-2: SELECT payment WHERE id='PAY-004' → version=0

  Thread-1: UPDATE payment SET status='PROCESSED', version=1 WHERE id='PAY-004' AND version=0
    → 1 row updated → SUCCESS (Recommended) 

  Thread-2: UPDATE payment SET status='PROCESSED', version=1 WHERE id='PAY-004' AND version=0
    → 0 rows updated (version is now 1, not 0!) → OptimisticLockException!
    → @Retryable: wait 100ms → re-read (version=1) → retry → SUCCESS (Recommended) 

  ═══ WHEN TO USE WHICH ═══

  SKIP LOCKED: queue-style processing. Multiple workers. Items can be processed in any order.
    → Best for: payment queues, job queues, notification queues.

  Optimistic (@Version + @Retryable): low-contention updates.
    → Best for: concurrent edits to different entities, rare conflicts.
    → Bad for: hot rows (constant retries = waste).

  Pessimistic (SELECT FOR UPDATE): high-contention hot rows.
    → Best for: balance updates, inventory decrements.
    → Must use consistent lock ordering to prevent AB-BA deadlocks.

  Lock ordering: always lock rows in deterministic order (alphabetical by ID).
    → Prevents AB-BA deadlocks with pessimistic locking.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Parallel transaction deadlocks are handled with four strategies depending on the use case. Consistent lock ordering prevents AB-BA deadlocks by ensuring all threads lock rows in the same deterministic order. Optimistic locking with Version avoids locks entirely: Hibernate checks the version on update and throws ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException if another transaction modified the row. Combined with Retryable, the failed transaction automatically retries with exponential backoff. SKIP LOCKED is ideal for queue-style processing: SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED picks the next available row and skips rows already locked by other transactions — zero waiting, zero deadlocks, zero duplicate processing.

In my payment queue service, multiple instances process pending payments concurrently using SKIP LOCKED. Each instance picks a different payment without conflicting with others. For scenarios like concurrent account balance updates where the same row is contested, we use pessimistic SELECT FOR UPDATE with consistent lock ordering by account ID. For low-contention scenarios where conflicts are rare, optimistic locking with Version and Retryable provides the best throughput because no database locks are held during the transaction — only a version check at commit time.
